title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
directAnswer: Breadth-first search with a queue, processing the tree one level at a time. Before each round, snapshot the queue's current size — that's exactly how many nodes are on this level. Dequeue that many, collect their values into a sub-list, and enqueue their children for the next round. O(n) time, O(n) space. The 'capture the level size up front' trick is what cleanly groups nodes by depth.

remember.pattern: BFS by level (snapshot the queue size)
rules: Snapshot `len(queue)` **before** the inner loop — appending children mid-loop would otherwise bleed the next level into this one.
Guard against a **null root**: return an empty list, don't enqueue null.
Use a real **queue/deque** with O(1) pop-from-front, not `list.pop(0)` which is O(n).
Enqueue children **left before right** so each level reads left-to-right.
Each node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once → O(n) time; the queue can hold a full level → O(n) space.
whenToUse: You need results grouped by **depth / level** of the tree
Anything that asks for 'level', 'row', 'each layer', or 'breadth'
Zigzag, right-side view, level averages — all are BFS-by-level variants
antiSignals: You only need a single value per level or just the last level → still BFS but lighter bookkeeping
Order doesn't matter and you just want all nodes → plain DFS is simpler
Tree is enormous and you only need depth → DFS recursion avoids the wide queue
You need pre/in/post order → that's DFS, not BFS
remember.takeaway: Level-order traversal is the canonical BFS-on-a-tree. The one idea that makes it click is fixing the level boundary by reading the queue size before you start dequeuing — every 'do something per level' tree problem (zigzag, right view, level averages, min depth) is a small twist on this skeleton.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know BFS uses a queue, and whether you can cleanly separate one level from the next using the queue-size snapshot rather than tagging nodes with depth.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Reading `len(queue)` inside the loop (so children get counted into the current level), or using `list.pop(0)` and quietly turning the traversal into O(n²).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the level-size trick explicitly, handle the empty tree first, and mention the DFS-with-depth alternative that produces the same grouping in O(h) stack space.

problemStatement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return ***the level order traversal*** of its nodes' values. (i.e., from left to right, level by level).

The result is a list of lists: the i-th inner list contains all node values at depth i, ordered left to right.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 2000]
The tree may be empty (root == null)
understanding: Produce the node values grouped by depth: row 0 is just the root, row 1 is its children left-to-right, and so on. We need a traversal that fans out one layer at a time and a way to know where each layer ends.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the tree be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — constraints allow 0 nodes. Return an empty list, and don't enqueue a null root.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Left-to-right within each level, or any order?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Left-to-right. Enqueue the left child before the right child so the queue preserves that order.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want a flat list or a list grouped by level?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Grouped — one inner list per depth. That's why we batch by the level size each round.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can the tree get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 2000 nodes here, but the BFS approach scales to any size in O(n); the widest level bounds the queue size.

examples.explanation: Depth 0 is [3]; depth 1 is [9,20]; depth 2 is the children of 20, namely [15,7].
A single node forms one level.

approaches.name: DFS with Depth Index
approaches.whenToMention: Offer it as the recursive alternative: it produces the same grouped output and uses only O(h) stack space instead of an O(width) queue.
hints: Could you recurse normally but also pass down which level you're on?
Carry a `depth` argument. The node at `depth` belongs in `result[depth]`.
If `result` doesn't yet have a list at index `depth`, create one, then append the node's value and recurse into both children with `depth + 1`.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Every node is visited once → O(n). The recursion stack reaches the tree's height → O(h), better than BFS's O(width) for tall, narrow trees (ignoring the output list itself).
approaches.explanation:
You don't strictly need a queue to group by level — a depth-carrying DFS works too. The key is that a node's depth tells you exactly which output row it belongs to.

**How the grouping happens.** We recurse pre-order (node, then left, then right) while tracking the current `depth`. The first time we reach a given depth, we append a fresh empty list to `result`. Because we always recurse left before right, values land in each row in left-to-right order automatically.

**Why left-before-right matters.** DFS doesn't visit a level contiguously — it dives all the way down the left spine first. But within any single depth, the left subtree's nodes are always reached before the right subtree's, so the per-row ordering still comes out left-to-right.

**Space trade-off vs BFS.** DFS holds at most one root-to-leaf path on the stack, O(h). BFS holds an entire level in the queue, O(width). For a balanced tree the widest level is ~n/2, so DFS can be more memory-friendly on tall trees, while BFS is more natural when the problem is fundamentally about levels.
approaches.insight: The depth argument is the whole trick: it's a stable key that maps each node to its output row regardless of visitation order. This 'pass an accumulator/index down the recursion' technique generalizes to many tree problems.

dryRun.intro: DFS pre-order carrying depth; result[depth] collects each node's value.

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
def levelOrder(self, root: 'TreeNode') -> list[list[int]]:
    result: list[list[int]] = []

    def dfs(node: 'TreeNode', depth: int) -> None:
        if node is None:
            return
        if depth == len(result):
            result.append([])
        result[depth].append(node.val)
        dfs(node.left, depth + 1)
        dfs(node.right, depth + 1)

    dfs(root, 0)
    return result

java.explanation: First time we reach this depth → create its row before appending.
Map the node to its level by index — depth is the row key.
Left before right keeps each row in left-to-right order.

python.explanation: Need a new row for a depth we haven't reached yet.
depth indexes directly into the grouped output.
Recurse left first so values fill rows left-to-right.

pitfalls: Recursing right before left — scrambles the within-level order.
Forgetting to create result[depth] the first time, causing an index error.
Assuming DFS visits levels contiguously — it doesn't, but the depth index still groups correctly.

approaches.name: BFS with a Queue — Level by Level (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The canonical answer. Lead with 'level order means BFS with a queue', then explain the size-snapshot trick.
hints: Level order means visiting nodes nearest the root first. What data structure gives you first-in-first-out exploration?
Push the root, then repeatedly process the queue. The trick: how do you know where one level ends and the next begins?

Before processing a level, record how many nodes are currently in the queue — that count is the size of the current level. Pop exactly that many, collecting values, and enqueue their children for next time.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once and does O(1) work → O(n) time. The queue holds at most one level; the widest level can be ~n/2 nodes → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
BFS is the textbook fit for 'process nearest-first', and a FIFO queue gives that ordering for free. The only added requirement here is grouping the output by depth, which the size-snapshot handles.

**The size-snapshot trick.** When we start a level, the queue contains exactly the nodes of that level and nothing else. We read `levelSize = queue.size()` once, then dequeue precisely that many nodes. As we dequeue each, we enqueue its children — but those children belong to the *next* level, and since we loop a fixed `levelSize` times, they aren't touched until the next round. This cleanly walls off one level from the next without storing a depth on each node.

**Why the snapshot must come before the loop.** If you re-read `queue.size()` inside the loop condition, the size grows as you append children, and the current level's sub-list absorbs nodes from deeper levels. Capturing the size up front freezes the boundary.

**Why a real queue matters.** We need O(1) removal from the front. In Python use `collections.deque` (`popleft` is O(1)); a plain list's `pop(0)` is O(n) and silently makes the whole traversal O(n²). In Java, `ArrayDeque` / `LinkedList` via the `Queue` interface gives O(1) `poll`.

**Handling the empty tree.** A null root means no levels at all. Guard it before the loop — enqueuing null and later dereferencing it is a classic crash.
approaches.insight: The queue size at the top of each iteration is a free 'level marker'. You don't need to tag nodes with their depth or push sentinels — the count of what's already enqueued *is* the level boundary. This single observation powers zigzag traversal, right-side view, and level averages with almost no change.

dryRun.intro: queue starts with [3]. Each round: snapshot size, drain that many, enqueue children.

code.python:
from collections import deque

# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
def levelOrder(self, root: 'TreeNode') -> list[list[int]]:
    result: list[list[int]] = []
    if not root:
        return result
    queue = deque([root])
    while queue:
        level_size = len(queue)
        level: list[int] = []
        for _ in range(level_size):
            node = queue.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)
            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)
        result.append(level)
    return result

java.explanation: Empty tree → no levels; return the empty result before touching the queue.
Snapshot the level boundary BEFORE adding children — the heart of the algorithm.
Drain exactly one level; children enqueued here belong to the next round.
Left before right preserves left-to-right level order.

python.explanation: Guard the null root so we never enqueue or dereference None.
Freeze how many nodes are on this level before the loop appends children.
deque.popleft is O(1); list.pop(0) would be O(n) and make this O(n²).
Enqueue children left-then-right for next level's ordering.

pitfalls: Re-reading queue.size() inside the loop so children leak into the current level.
Using list.pop(0) in Python — O(n) per pop turns the traversal into O(n²).
Enqueuing a null root and then dereferencing it.

commonMistakes: Reading the queue size inside the loop instead of snapshotting it before — merges adjacent levels.
Using list.pop(0) for the queue, quietly degrading to O(n²).
Forgetting the empty-tree guard and enqueuing a null root.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Reading the level size inside the loop
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The queue grows as you enqueue children, so a loop bounded by the live size keeps consuming next-level nodes into the current row, collapsing all levels into one.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using a list as a queue
commonMistakesDetailed.why: list.pop(0) shifts every remaining element left, costing O(n) each call. Over n nodes that's O(n²). A deque (Python) or ArrayDeque/LinkedList (Java) pops from the front in O(1).
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
from collections import deque
queue = deque([root])
while queue:
    node = queue.popleft()  # O(1)
